title: Preface to curvature
one_line_summary: Physical arguments (redshift, equivalence principle, tides) show gravity forbids global inertial frames and points to curved spacetime; the chapter then builds the whole toolkit of covariant differentiation (Christoffel symbols, metric compatibility, Gamma from the metric) inside the flat Euclidean plane using polar coordinates.
role_in_book: This is the hinge between the special-relativity half of the book (chapters 1-4: Lorentz frames, one-forms and tensors, fluids and MCRFs) and the geometry of curved manifolds in chapter 6. Section 5.1 supplies the physical reason curvature is needed: energy conservation forces a gravitational redshift, the redshift rules out a Lorentz frame at rest on Earth, universality of free fall promotes freely falling frames to inertial status, and tidal nonuniformity restricts those frames to be local, which matches the local flatness of Riemannian geometry. Sections 5.2-5.5 then deliberately retreat to a flat plane with curvilinear coordinates, where Cartesian coordinates provide ground truth, to develop coordinate transformations, bases that vary from point to point, the metric in non-Cartesian coordinates, Christoffel symbols, covariant derivatives of all tensor types, the identity that the metric is covariantly constant, the formula for Gamma in terms of metric derivatives, and the distinction between coordinate and noncoordinate bases. Chapter 6 carries these results over nearly unchanged to curved manifolds. What it adds is local flatness made precise, parallel transport and geodesics, and the Riemann tensor.

assumed_background.topic: Invariant interval and the Minkowski metric as encoding rod lengths and clock readings
Doppler shift formula for light between relatively moving frames
One-forms, gradient one-form, (0 2) tensors built from basis one-forms, index raising and lowering with the metric
Momentarily comoving reference frames (MCRFs) and the flux vector N
Newtonian gravity, free fall with constant g, kinetic energy, and the origin of ocean tides
Photon energy E = h nu and mass-energy equivalence
Plane polar coordinates and trigonometric identities
Partial derivatives, chain rule, equality of mixed partial derivatives, Taylor expansion
Divergence and Laplacian in Cartesian and (as a formula to be re-derived) polar coordinates
Matrix multiplication, inverse matrices, determinants, row versus column vectors
Euclid's parallel postulate and great circles on a sphere

learning_objectives: Reader can derive the first-order gravitational redshift 1 - gh from a no-perpetual-motion argument with a tower, a falling mass and a returning photon.
Reader can reproduce Schild's spacetime-diagram argument that a static laboratory on Earth cannot be a Lorentz frame, given the measured redshift.

Reader can explain why universality of free fall makes freely falling frames the natural inertial frames, state the weak and Einstein equivalence principles, and show to first order that a freely falling observer sees no redshift.
Reader can explain why tidal nonuniformity limits inertial frames to small regions of space and time and connect this to local flatness and to geodesics that fail to stay parallel.

Reader can test whether a coordinate transformation is admissible using its Jacobian and write the transformation matrices for vectors and one-forms as partial derivatives, verifying that they are mutual inverses.
Reader can define a curve as a parametrized path, compute its tangent vector, and interpret a vector as the operator that returns the derivative of a scalar along the curve.

Reader can compute the polar coordinate basis vectors and basis one-forms, their magnitudes, the metric components diag(1, r^2), the inverse metric, and the line element, and distinguish the one-form gradient from the vector gradient.
Reader can compute derivatives of the polar basis vectors, read off all Christoffel symbols of polar coordinates, and assemble the covariant derivative of a vector field as a (1 1) tensor.
Reader can derive the divergence and the Laplacian in plane polar coordinates from contraction of the covariant derivative.

Reader can write the covariant derivative of one-forms and arbitrary tensors (one Gamma term per index with sign fixed by index position) and justify the one-form rule via the product rule on a contraction.

Reader can prove that the metric is covariantly constant, that Christoffel symbols are symmetric in a coordinate basis, and derive the formula for Gamma in terms of first derivatives of the metric, then apply it to polar coordinates.
Reader can explain in what sense Christoffel symbols are and are not tensor components.

Reader can construct the orthonormal polar basis, prove via mixed partial derivatives that it is not a coordinate basis, and convert between coordinate-basis and orthonormal-basis components to reconcile vector-calculus textbook formulas.

teaching_approach.summary: The chapter has two halves with different styles. The first is a chain of physical thought experiments, each forcing the next conclusion: energy conservation implies redshift; redshift plus a static field forbids a Lorentz frame on Earth; universality of free fall picks out freely falling frames; nonuniform fields make those frames only local; failure of free world lines to stay parallel is identified with curvature. The second half is a patient, component-level but geometrically interpreted construction of tensor calculus in the one setting where the learner can always check the answer: the Euclidean plane in polar coordinates. Every new object (basis vectors, one-forms, metric components, Christoffel symbols, covariant derivative, metric compatibility) is computed explicitly for polar coordinates and cross-checked against Cartesian results or familiar vector-calculus formulas, and general statements are promoted using the argument that an equation between tensors true in Cartesian coordinates holds in every coordinate system.
narrative_arc: Motivating question: SR's metric is defined by rods and clocks in a global inertial frame; can such a frame exist when gravity is present?
Energy-conservation thought experiment on a tower predicts that a climbing photon loses the fraction gh of its energy; Pound-Rebka-Snider and GPS confirm it.

Schild's argument: in a static field, successive wave crests follow congruent world lines, so a Minkowski lab frame would give equal crest spacings at top and bottom, contradicting the measured redshift; the Earth frame is not inertial.

Universality of free fall means no particle can mark an unaccelerated frame at rest on Earth; freely falling frames are the candidates; the accelerating rocket runs the argument backwards and yields the equivalence principle (weak and Einstein forms).
Check: in a frame that begins falling when the photon is emitted, the Doppler shift exactly cancels the gravitational shift to first order, so no redshift is seen.

Limitation: frames falling at different places around Earth move in different directions and at different rates, so only local inertial frames exist; the nonuniformity (tidal force) is the true signature of gravity.

Geometric reinterpretation: parallel free world lines stay parallel in flat Minkowski space but not in a nonuniform field; like the sphere, spacetime is locally flat but curved, and free-fall paths are geodesics.
Strategic retreat: learn the mathematics of curvature first in curvilinear coordinates on the flat Euclidean plane, focusing on parallelism rather than metrics.
Formalism I: coordinate transformations and the Jacobian, one-forms defined from gradients of scalars, vectors as tangents to parametrized curves, transformation matrices as partial derivatives.
Formalism II: polar basis vectors and one-forms vary in direction and length from point to point; metric components, line element, inverse metric, and vector versus one-form gradient.
Formalism III: differentiating a vector requires differentiating the basis; Christoffel symbols encode basis derivatives; covariant derivative components form a single (1 1) tensor.
Payoff check: divergence and Laplacian in polar coordinates fall out of contraction.
Extension: covariant derivatives of one-forms and higher tensors via the product rule on scalars; systematic one-Gamma-per-index rule.
Metric enters: metric compatibility from the Cartesian-then-tensor-equation argument, explicit check in polars, symmetry of Gamma, and inversion to Gamma from metric derivatives.
Clarification: Gamma are components of a family of tensors nabla e_alpha but not of one tensor, so they do not transform tensorially.
Noncoordinate bases: orthonormal polar basis fails integrability; which results survive; why vector-calculus books get different-looking formulas.
Look ahead: what is missing is a quantitative measure of the failure of parallelism, the Riemann tensor.
signature_moves: Derives the gravitational redshift from forbidding perpetual motion before any relativistic gravity theory is written down.
Draws the light crests on a deliberately arbitrary curved path so the conclusion depends only on time-independence of the field, not on how gravity bends light.
Turns the equivalence principle around by describing gravity-free acceleration of a rocket, which learners find more familiar than free fall.
Verifies the candidate inertial frame by computing that the free-fall Doppler shift cancels the redshift to first order.

Defines flatness and curvature through the fate of initially parallel free-particle world lines (Euclid's axiom) rather than through the metric, and insists the chapter is about parallelism, not metrics.
Builds all of tensor calculus in the flat plane with polar coordinates, where Cartesian coordinates are always available to check every result.
Promotes results with the pattern: prove it trivially in Cartesian coordinates, observe it is a tensor equation, conclude it holds in all coordinates.

Treats the one-form (gradient) as the foundational object and defines vectors as tangents to curves that produce d phi/ds, the modern view, in contrast to transforming-like-a-displacement definitions.
Explains non-unit polar basis lengths physically: e_theta must span one radian, so it grows with r, while d-tilde-theta grows near the origin.
Uses the constant vector e_x having non-constant polar components as the motivating paradox for Christoffel symbols.
Re-derives the textbook polar Laplacian as a reward for the formalism.

Gives a mnemonic for covariant-derivative index placement (derivative index last, one Gamma per index, sign by up or down) and a reason for the sign (contraction of basis one-forms and vectors is constant).
Takes a nuanced stance on whether Christoffel symbols are tensors instead of the blunt textbook denial.
Reconciles the reader's prior vector-calculus formulas by exposing that those books silently use a noncoordinate orthonormal basis.

sections.title: On the relation of gravitation to curvature
sections.summary: Opens by recalling that SR rests on global inertial frames whose metric is physically defined by clocks and rods, then tests whether gravity allows such frames. Subsections: the gravitational redshift from a tower thought experiment and its confirmation (Pound-Rebka-Snider, GPS); Schild's proof that no Lorentz frame is at rest on Earth; the principle of equivalence (universality of free fall, rocket, weak vs Einstein versions, locality, many freely falling frames); the redshift re-examined in a freely falling frame (none to first order); local inertial frames limited by nonuniformity (Figure 5.3); tidal forces as the essence of gravity; and the role of curvature, where non-parallel free world lines, local flatness of Riemannian spaces, and Einstein's identification of free-fall paths with geodesics motivate a study of curvature, begun in flat space with curvilinear coordinates.
concepts: nonexistence of a Lorentz frame at rest on Earth
flat versus curved geometry via parallelism
key_moves: Mass m dropped from height h arrives with energy m + mgh; converted to a photon and sent up, it must arrive with energy m, otherwise a perpetual-motion engine results; hence E'/E = 1 - gh.

In a static field the second crest's world line is a time translate of the first; Minkowski geometry would then give equal crest intervals at bottom and top, but frequency is higher at the bottom, so the lab frame is not Lorentz.
Gravity affects all bodies identically, so no free particle can define rest in a non-falling frame; a freely falling frame keeps free particles at uniform velocity.
Rocket in empty space: dropped objects fall together and held objects have weight proportional to mass, so uniform gravity is equivalent to uniform acceleration.
Weak equivalence principle concerns motion under gravity alone; Einstein's version asserts all local laws take their SR form in freely falling frames (used in chapter 7).
Free-fall frame starting at rest at emission acquires speed gh during the light travel time h; the Doppler factor (1+gh)/sqrt(1-g^2h^2) cancels the redshift to first order.
Frames falling toward Earth at different points converge and fall at different rates with height, so a rigid global freely falling frame is impossible; inertial frames are local, like MCRFs.
Tidal forces are defined as field nonuniformities and are taken as the fundamental manifestation of gravity.

Minkowski space is flat (parallel free world lines remain parallel) but non-Euclidean (null lines have zero length); nonuniform gravity breaks parallelism, so spacetime is curved yet locally flat like a sphere.
Plan: study curvilinear coordinates on the flat plane to develop the tools; emphasis on parallelism, not metrics.

sections.title: Tensor algebra in polar coordinates
sections.summary: Introduces general coordinates on the Euclidean plane with polar coordinates as the running example. Shows how coordinate increments transform, requires a nonvanishing Jacobian, and contrasts the old definition of vectors (transform like displacements) with the modern one built on one-forms defined as gradients of scalar fields, whose transformation law follows from the chain rule and acts on row vectors. Distinguishes paths from curves (parametrized paths), defines tangent vectors and the interpretation of a vector as the thing that produces d phi/ds from d-tilde-phi. Computes the polar basis vectors and basis one-forms, observes that they change direction and magnitude from point to point, computes the metric components diag(1, r^2), the line element dr^2 + r^2 d theta^2 (warning against confusing it with the tensor d-tilde-r tensor d-tilde-r + r^2 d-tilde-theta tensor d-tilde-theta), the inverse metric, and the vector gradient, whose components differ from those of the one-form gradient except in Cartesian coordinates.
concepts: transformation matrices for vectors and one-forms
coordinate basis vectors and basis one-forms in polar coordinates
inverse metric and the vector gradient
key_moves: Increments Delta r and Delta theta are linear in Delta x and Delta y to first order (Eq. 5.4); a general coordinate map needs a nonzero Jacobian to assign distinct labels to distinct points.

One-form d-tilde-phi is defined by its components (partial derivatives of phi) in any coordinates; the chain rule gives its transformation with matrix Lambda^alpha_beta' = dx^alpha/dx^beta', summed on the first index.
The vector and one-form transformation matrices multiply to the identity by the chain rule.
A curve is a map from an interval to the plane; reparametrizing gives a new curve with the same path; the tangent V with components d xi/ds, d eta/ds satisfies d phi/ds = <d-tilde-phi, V>.
e_r = cos theta e_x + sin theta e_y, e_theta = -r sin theta e_x + r cos theta e_y; d-tilde-r and d-tilde-theta follow analogously; transformation matrix entries are fixed by index placement.
|e_theta| = r because e_theta represents a displacement of one radian; |d-tilde-theta| = 1/r.
g_alpha'beta' = e_alpha' . e_beta' gives g_rr = 1, g_theta theta = r^2, g_r theta = 0; line element dl^2 = dr^2 + r^2 d theta^2.
Inverse metric diag(1, r^-2) raises the gradient: vector gradient has components (phi_,r , phi_,theta / r^2).

sections.title: Tensor calculus in polar coordinates
sections.summary: Starts from the paradox that the constant vector e_x has polar components (cos theta, -sin theta / r) that vary, so differentiating components alone cannot give the derivative of a vector. Computes derivatives of the polar basis vectors (with Figure 5.6 as a picture), checks that the product rule including basis derivatives yields d e_x / d theta = 0, and defines Christoffel symbols as the components of basis-vector derivatives. Tabulates all polar Christoffel symbols, assembles the covariant derivative V^alpha_;beta and interprets it as the components of a single (1 1) tensor nabla V computable either directly with Gamma or by transforming from Cartesian coordinates. Covariant derivative of a scalar is the gradient. Divergence follows by contraction, giving the polar divergence and Laplacian formulas. The covariant derivative of a one-form is derived from the product rule applied to the scalar p_alpha V^alpha, and the pattern is extended to tensors of any rank.
concepts: covariant derivative of one-forms and higher-rank tensors
key_moves: Differentiate e_r and e_theta using constancy of e_x and e_y: d e_r/dr = 0, d e_r/d theta = e_theta / r, d e_theta/dr = e_theta / r, d e_theta/d theta = -r e_r.
Expand e_x in polar basis and differentiate with the product rule; component-derivative terms and basis-derivative terms cancel to give zero.
Write d V/dx^beta = (dV^alpha/dx^beta) e_alpha + V^alpha d e_alpha/dx^beta; define Gamma^mu_alpha beta by d e_alpha/dx^beta = Gamma^mu_alpha beta e_mu.
Relabel dummy indices to factor out e_alpha: V^alpha_;beta = V^alpha_,beta + V^mu Gamma^alpha_mu beta.
Regard beta as a slot: nabla V maps e_beta to d V/dx^beta, a (1 1) tensor; its components in any system can be computed directly or by tensor transformation from Cartesian.
Contraction is frame invariant, so V^alpha_;alpha in polars equals the Cartesian divergence; with Gamma^alpha_r alpha = 1/r this is (1/r) d(r V^r)/dr + d V^theta/d theta.
Raise the gradient then take divergence to get the polar Laplacian.

Apply the product rule to phi = p_alpha V^alpha, substitute V^alpha_;beta, and identify the remaining bracket as a tensor component, which defines the one-form covariant derivative with a minus-sign Gamma term (Eq. 5.63).
Generalize: add a +Gamma term for each upper index and a -Gamma term for each lower index.

sections.title: Christoffel symbols and the metric
sections.summary: Brings the metric into the covariant derivative. Because in Cartesian coordinates a vector and its associated one-form have equal components and nabla just differentiates components, lowering an index commutes with covariant differentiation; being a tensor statement, this holds in all coordinates, and comparing with the product rule shows the metric is covariantly constant. The identity is checked explicitly for g_theta theta;r in polar coordinates. A perspective paragraph notes that metric compatibility will persist in curved spaces. Symmetry of Christoffel symbols in their lower indices is proven from the symmetry of the second covariant derivative of a scalar. Three permutations of the compatibility equation are combined to solve for Gamma in terms of metric derivatives, checked on Gamma^theta_r theta = 1/r. The section ends by explaining that Gamma^mu_alpha beta are components of the (1 1) tensors nabla e_alpha, one per basis vector, but not of one (1 2) tensor, which is why they do not obey the tensor transformation law.
key_moves: In Cartesian coordinates, nabla_beta of the one-form associated with V equals g(nabla_beta V, .) because components are equal and Gamma = 0; as a tensor equation it holds everywhere: V_alpha;beta = g_alpha mu V^mu_;beta.
Covariantly differentiate V_alpha = g_alpha mu V^mu with the product rule and compare, for arbitrary V, to conclude g_alpha mu;beta = 0.
Explicit check in polar coordinates: g_theta theta;r = 2r - r - r = 0.

Second covariant derivative of a scalar is symmetric in Cartesian coordinates, hence in all; with partial derivatives commuting, Gamma^mu_alpha beta phi_,mu is symmetric for arbitrary phi, so Gamma is symmetric.
Write compatibility for three index permutations, add two and subtract one, use symmetry of Gamma and g, divide by 2 and contract with g^alpha gamma to obtain Gamma from metric derivatives.
Recompute Gamma^theta_r theta from g_theta theta = r^2 to check.
Changing coordinates changes which tensors nabla e_alpha are relevant, so Gamma does not transform as a single tensor; Gamma vanishes in Cartesian but not polar coordinates.

sections.title: Noncoordinate bases
sections.summary: Shows that not every field of bases arises from coordinates. The polar coordinate basis is not unit; the normalized basis e_r-hat = e_r, e_theta-hat = e_theta / r with dual one-forms d-tilde-r and r d-tilde-theta is orthonormal. Asking whether coordinates (xi, eta) generate it reduces, via the one-forms, to requiring partial derivatives of eta equal to -sin theta and cos theta, whose mixed partials disagree, so the basis is noncoordinate. Vector-calculus textbooks use this orthonormal basis, which explains why their divergence formula differs from Eq. 5.56 by the factor relating components. In a noncoordinate basis the comma no longer means a partial derivative with respect to a coordinate, Christoffel symbols can still be defined but are not symmetric, and the metric formula for Gamma fails. The general criterion is an integrability condition on the transformation matrix. Coordinate bases are simpler and used throughout the book; orthonormal bases are popular because the metric is the identity, but the only orthonormal coordinate basis in flat space is Cartesian.
key_moves: Normalize the polar basis to get e_r-hat and e_theta-hat and dual one-forms; verify orthonormality.
Assume the orthonormal one-forms are gradients d-tilde-xi, d-tilde-eta; express them in Cartesian one-forms to get d eta/dx = -sin theta, d eta/dy = cos theta.
Require equality of mixed partials; the condition fails (the left-hand combination equals 1/r), so no such eta exists.
Coordinate-basis components (a, b) become orthonormal components (a, r b); the divergence formula changes accordingly to Eq. 5.87, with no contradiction.
Define phi_,mu as d-tilde-phi(e_mu); in the orthonormal basis phi_,theta-hat = (1/r) d phi/d theta, not a partial derivative.
Symmetry of Gamma and Eq. 5.75 rely on commuting partial derivatives and so hold only in coordinate bases (generalization deferred to Exercise 5.20).
A basis is a coordinate basis only if its transformation matrix satisfies the integrability conditions (curl-free rows).

sections.title: Looking ahead
sections.summary: Short bridge: the notation and concepts needed for curved spaces are now almost all in hand, and sections 5.2-5.4 are the template for the next chapter. The missing ingredient is a careful account of parallelism and a quantitative measure of how badly Euclid's parallel axiom fails, which will be the Riemann curvature tensor.
key_moves: Flags §§5.2-5.4 as essential because curvature will be developed by analogy.
Names the Riemann tensor as the measure of the failure of parallelism.

sections.title: Bibliography
sections.summary: Points to sources on the experimental foundations of GR (Eötvös and Pound-Rebka-Snider experiments: Dicke 1964, Misner, Thorne and Wheeler 1973, Will 2014 and 2018), a nonmathematical motivation for curvature (Hoffmann 1983), relativity in GPS (Ashby 2003), and mathematical treatments of curvilinear coordinates and differential geometry (Abraham et al. 1988, Lovelock and Rund 1990, Schutz 1980b).

sections.title: Exercises
sections.summary: Twenty-two exercises spanning a more realistic redshift engine, tides in a uniform field, Jacobians of candidate transformations, curves and reparametrization, polar transformation matrices, transforming scalars, vectors and one-forms, computing covariant derivatives three ways and checking divergence, second covariant derivatives, the Gamma-from-metric derivation, transformation law of Gamma, orthonormal bases, commutation coefficients for noncoordinate bases, Rindler coordinates for a uniformly accelerated observer, and index lowering through a directional derivative.
key_moves: Several exercises chain together (5.7 -> 5.8 -> 5.11, 5.12 -> 5.13) so the same fields are handled by direct and transformation methods and the answers must agree.

concepts.name: gravitational redshift
concepts.definition: Light climbing a height h in a gravitational field of strength g arrives with frequency (and energy) reduced by the fractional amount gh/c^2 to first order; equivalently clocks higher in the field run faster as seen from below.
concepts.how_introduced: Derived without any theory of gravity from an idealized tower: a mass falls, gains energy mgh, is converted into a photon sent upward and reconverted to mass at the top. Forbidding perpetual motion requires the photon to lose exactly the energy gained, giving E'/E = 1 - gh (units c = 1). Then confirmed by Pound-Rebka-Snider and GPS, and reinterpreted as a Doppler shift seen from a freely falling frame.
concepts.notes: The O(v^4) notation reflects that gh is of order v^2 for the falling mass. The book states only the first-order result.

concepts.name: Pound-Rebka-Snider experiment
concepts.definition: Laboratory measurement (1960, improved 1965) of the gravitational frequency shift of gamma rays over a vertical height of 22.5 m, using the Mössbauer effect for extreme frequency resolution; agreed with the predicted gh shift to about 1%.
concepts.how_introduced: Cited immediately after the tower thought experiment as direct confirmation, then reused as the physical input to Schild's argument (measured nu_bottom > nu_top).

concepts.name: nonexistence of a Lorentz frame at rest on Earth
concepts.definition: Given a time-independent gravitational field and the observed redshift, a frame at rest relative to Earth cannot have Minkowski geometry, because congruent world lines of successive light crests would force equal crest intervals at bottom and top, contradicting the measured frequency difference.
concepts.how_introduced: Spacetime diagram (Figure 5.2) with height on the horizontal axis; tower bottom and top are vertical lines; two crests are drawn on arbitrary wiggly curves so that no assumption about how gravity bends light is made. Static field implies the second path is a time translate of the first; in Minkowski geometry this gives equal Delta t, but Delta t = 1/nu differs.
prerequisites: time-translation invariance of a static field

concepts.notes: Attributed to Schild (1967). The argument shows the Earth frame is not inertial, not that inertial frames do not exist.

concepts.name: universality of free fall
aliases: equality of inertial and gravitational mass
concepts.definition: All test bodies started with the same position and velocity follow the same trajectory in a gravitational field regardless of mass or composition.
concepts.how_introduced: Contrasted with electromagnetism (charge-to-mass ratio dependence) and the strong and weak interactions, which act selectively and so permit an unaffected particle to mark an inertial frame; gravity does not, so no particle can mark a non-falling inertial frame on Earth. Galileo's Pisa experiment is invoked; a footnote points to the Eötvös experiment.

concepts.name: weak equivalence principle
aliases: principle of equivalence between gravity and acceleration
concepts.definition: Motion of bodies under gravity alone is locally indistinguishable from motion viewed from a uniformly accelerated frame: a uniform gravitational field is equivalent to uniform acceleration relative to inertial frames, and freely falling frames are locally inertial for free particles.
concepts.how_introduced: First argued forward (freely falling frames keep free particles at uniform velocity), then turned around with a rocket accelerating in empty space: dropped objects fall together toward the rear and held objects have weight proportional to mass. Called weak because it concerns only gravitational motion; noted as already a foundation of Newtonian gravity.

concepts.name: Einstein equivalence principle
aliases: the book's 'stronger form' of the equivalence principle
concepts.definition: In a freely falling local inertial frame, the differential equations expressing all nongravitational laws of physics take the same local form as in special relativity; this tells how every force behaves in a gravitational field.
concepts.how_introduced: Stated briefly as Einstein's extension of the weak principle beyond particle motion, with a forward pointer to its use in chapter 7.
concepts.notes: Schutz calls this a stronger form of the principle than the weak one. It should not be confused with the modern 'strong equivalence principle', which also covers self-gravitating bodies and gravitational experiments.

concepts.name: local inertial frame
concepts.definition: A freely falling reference frame that behaves as an inertial frame of special relativity only within a region of space and time small enough that nonuniformities of the gravitational field are undetectable; mathematically, inertial at a point.
concepts.how_introduced: Once freely falling frames are shown to see no redshift, the book asks how far such a frame can extend. Figure 5.3 draws a lattice falling toward Earth: only the row through B, aimed at Earth's centre, moves along a genuine free-fall path; rows A and C would have to fall obliquely toward the centre, so a rigid lattice cannot follow them. Because g also changes with distance from Earth, parts of the lattice nearer and farther from Earth would need different accelerations, and both problems worsen as the fall proceeds. The limitation is likened to an MCRF of a fluid (valid only locally and momentarily); how small the region must be depends on the field's nonuniformity and the sensitivity of the experiment, and any theory of gravity must admit frames that are inertial at a point.
concepts.notes: There are infinitely many local inertial frames at each event, differing by velocity and spatial orientation.

concepts.name: tidal forces
concepts.definition: The differences in gravitational acceleration between nearby points; they cannot be removed by going to a freely falling frame and are regarded in GR as the fundamental, frame-independent manifestation of gravity.
concepts.how_introduced: Named after ocean tides: a uniform field would make Earth fall freely with no tides, and tidal bulges come from the difference in lunar and solar pull across Earth's diameter. Identified as exactly what prevents global inertial frames.
concepts.notes: Made quantitative later via geodesic deviation and the Riemann tensor.

concepts.name: flat versus curved geometry via parallelism
aliases: Euclid's parallel postulate as flatness criterion
flat non-Euclidean geometry of Minkowski space
concepts.definition: A space is flat if locally straight lines (geodesics) that start parallel remain parallel everywhere (Euclid's axiom holds); it is curved if they do not. Flatness is distinct from being Euclidean: Minkowski space is flat but has an indefinite metric with null straight lines.
concepts.how_introduced: Free-particle world lines are the probe: in SR initially parallel ones stay parallel, so Minkowski space is flat; in a nonuniform field nearby free world lines diverge or converge, so spacetime is curved. The sphere, where great circles always meet, is the Euclidean-signature example.
concepts.notes: Sets up the chapter's stated emphasis on parallelism rather than metrics.

concepts.name: local flatness
concepts.definition: In any Riemannian space, a sufficiently small neighbourhood of any point can be treated as flat to good accuracy even though the space is globally curved.
concepts.how_introduced: Map analogy: a town map on flat paper is accurate, a flat map of the whole globe is badly distorted. Presented as the geometric counterpart of the existence of local inertial frames.
prerequisites: flat versus curved geometry via parallelism
concepts.notes: Riemann (1826-1866) credited in a footnote. Made precise in chapter 6.

concepts.name: geodesic
concepts.definition: A curve that is locally straight in a (possibly curved) geometry; in GR the world lines of freely falling particles are identified with the geodesics of curved spacetime.
concepts.how_introduced: Introduced informally as the generalization of straight lines on a sphere (great circles), then Einstein's key identification: free-fall paths are straight in local inertial frames but fail to stay parallel globally, just like geodesics.
concepts.notes: Formal definition via parallel transport comes in chapter 6.

concepts.name: curvilinear coordinate transformation
concepts.definition: A smooth invertible relabelling of points of the plane, (x, y) -> (xi(x,y), eta(x,y)), whose increments are related to Cartesian increments linearly to first order by the matrix of partial derivatives.
concepts.how_introduced: Polar coordinates are the concrete case (Eqs. 5.3-5.4), then generalized to arbitrary (xi, eta), with the bad example xi = x, eta = 1 showing distinct points can collapse to one label.

concepts.name: Jacobian of a coordinate transformation
concepts.definition: The determinant of the matrix of partial derivatives of new coordinates with respect to old; a transformation is locally one-to-one where it is nonzero and singular where it vanishes.
concepts.how_introduced: Motivated by requiring that zero coordinate increments imply zero displacement, i.e. the linear system (5.5) has only the trivial null solution.
concepts.notes: Polar coordinates are singular at r = 0 (Exercise 5.3).

concepts.name: transformation matrices for vectors and one-forms
concepts.definition: In general coordinates the vector transformation matrix is Lambda^alpha'_beta = dx^alpha'/dx^beta and the one-form matrix is Lambda^alpha_beta' = dx^alpha/dx^beta'; they are position-dependent inverses of one another, and index placement alone tells which derivative to use.
concepts.how_introduced: Vector law from displacement transformation (Eq. 5.7); one-form law from the chain rule on gradients written as a row vector multiplying a matrix (Eq. 5.12), so summation is on the first index. Inverse relation verified by multiplying matrices and using the chain rule. Noted that Lorentz matrices were symmetric, hiding the row/column distinction in SR.

concepts.name: gradient one-form
aliases: one-form as foundation of tensor algebra
concepts.definition: For a scalar field phi, the one-form whose components in any coordinates are the partial derivatives of phi; its transformation law follows automatically from the chain rule.
concepts.how_introduced: Presented as the modern foundation: instead of defining one vector (the displacement) and others by analogy, a whole class of one-forms is defined from derivatives, and vectors are then linear maps of one-forms to numbers. Basis one-forms d-tilde-r, d-tilde-theta are drawn as families of constant-r and constant-theta curves.

concepts.name: curve versus path
concepts.definition: A path is a set of points; a curve is a map from a real interval into the space, i.e. a path with a parameter value attached to each point. Reparametrizing gives a different curve with the same path.
concepts.how_introduced: Adopts modern mathematical terminology; Figure 5.4 shows parameter tick marks s = 1..8 along a path. Emphasizes that infinitely many curves share a path.

concepts.name: tangent vector
concepts.definition: The vector with components (d xi/ds, d eta/ds) associated with a parametrized curve; contracted with d-tilde-phi it gives the rate of change d phi/ds of any scalar along the curve, which is why it can be identified with the operator d/ds.
concepts.how_introduced: Derived from d phi/ds = <d-tilde-phi, V>: the one-form depends only on phi, the vector only on the curve. Components transform like displacements under coordinate changes since s is coordinate-independent. A path has many parallel tangents of different lengths (one per parametrization); V(s) reaches roughly from s to s+1.
concepts.notes: Book mentions but does not adopt the d/ds notation.

concepts.name: coordinate basis vectors and basis one-forms in polar coordinates
concepts.definition: e_r = cos theta e_x + sin theta e_y and e_theta = -r sin theta e_x + r cos theta e_y point along increasing r and theta; the dual one-forms are d-tilde-r = cos theta d-tilde-x + sin theta d-tilde-y and d-tilde-theta = (-sin theta d-tilde-x + cos theta d-tilde-y)/r.
concepts.how_introduced: Computed from e_alpha' = Lambda^beta_alpha' e_beta with Lambda entries as partial derivatives; one-forms computed analogously with a nod to the ordinary calculus increments (Eq. 5.4). Figure 5.5 draws the vectors at three points and the one-forms as short segments of constant-r and constant-theta curves.
prerequisites: transformation matrices for vectors and one-forms

concepts.name: position-dependent basis
concepts.definition: In curvilinear coordinates the basis vectors and one-forms change direction and magnitude from point to point; for polar coordinates |e_r| = 1, |e_theta| = r, |d-tilde-r| = 1, |d-tilde-theta| = 1/r.
concepts.how_introduced: Flagged as a point of great importance using Figure 5.5 (bases at A and C not parallel). Lengths explained physically: e_theta represents a one-radian displacement, which is longer far from the origin; d-tilde-theta is larger near the origin because a given vector sweeps more angle there.
prerequisites: coordinate basis vectors and basis one-forms in polar coordinates
concepts.notes: This variation, not curvature, is what forces Christoffel symbols in flat space.

concepts.name: metric tensor in polar coordinates
concepts.definition: The Euclidean metric tensor, whose Cartesian components are delta_alpha beta, has polar components g_alpha'beta' = e_alpha' . e_beta', namely g_rr = 1, g_theta theta = r^2, g_r theta = 0.
concepts.how_introduced: Computed directly as dot products of the polar basis vectors using the Cartesian metric; the same tensor, different components.
prerequisites: coordinate basis vectors and basis one-forms in polar coordinates

concepts.name: line element
aliases: ds^2 as display of metric components
concepts.definition: The squared length of an infinitesimal displacement written in terms of coordinate differentials, e.g. dl^2 = dr^2 + r^2 d theta^2; a compact display of metric components together with the coordinates used.
concepts.how_introduced: Obtained as |dr e_r + d theta e_theta|^2, then contrasted with the tensor g = d-tilde-r (x) d-tilde-r + r^2 d-tilde-theta (x) d-tilde-theta, which is an operator that yields dl^2 when fed the displacement twice; the book admits the notations look confusingly alike but keeps the traditional form.
concepts.notes: Here d means an infinitesimal coordinate increment, not the basis one-form.

concepts.name: inverse metric and the vector gradient
concepts.definition: The inverse metric g^alpha beta (polar: g^rr = 1, g^theta theta = 1/r^2) maps one-forms to vectors; the vector gradient of phi has polar components (d phi/dr, r^-2 d phi/d theta), different from the one-form components (d phi/dr, d phi/d theta).
concepts.how_introduced: Invert diag(1, r^2) and apply to the gradient one-form; conclusion drawn that even in Euclidean space vectors and their one-forms have different components except in Cartesian coordinates.
concepts.notes: Needed later for the polar Laplacian.

concepts.name: derivatives of basis vectors
concepts.definition: Since polar basis vectors vary with position, their partial derivatives with respect to the coordinates are nonzero vectors: d e_r/dr = 0, d e_r/d theta = e_theta/r, d e_theta/dr = e_theta/r, d e_theta/d theta = -r e_r.
concepts.how_introduced: Motivated by the paradox that the constant field e_x has non-constant polar components (cos theta, -sin theta/r), so component derivatives alone cannot give the vector derivative. Computed by differentiating Cartesian expansions with constant e_x, e_y, and pictured in Figure 5.6 as the small difference between nearby radial unit vectors, which points along e_theta.
prerequisites: coordinate basis vectors and basis one-forms in polar coordinates

concepts.name: Christoffel symbols
concepts.definition: The coefficients Gamma^mu_alpha beta defined by d e_alpha/dx^beta = Gamma^mu_alpha beta e_mu: the mu-th component of the rate of change of basis vector e_alpha along coordinate x^beta. For polar coordinates the only nonzero ones are Gamma^theta_r theta = Gamma^theta_theta r = 1/r and Gamma^r_theta theta = -r.
concepts.how_introduced: Named after noticing that the basis-derivative term in the vector derivative is a vector and so can be expanded in the basis. Index roles spelled out (which basis vector, which coordinate, which component). Polar values read off from the basis derivatives; emphasized that once computed they let one work entirely in polar coordinates without reference to Cartesian vectors.
concepts.notes: Tensor status deliberately postponed to §5.4.

concepts.name: covariant derivative of a vector
concepts.definition: The components of the derivative of a vector field along coordinate x^beta, including the change of basis: V^alpha_;beta = V^alpha_,beta + V^mu Gamma^alpha_mu beta.
concepts.how_introduced: Product rule on V = V^alpha e_alpha, substitute the Christoffel definition, relabel dummy indices to factor out e_alpha, and name the bracket with a semicolon.

concepts.name: covariant derivative tensor nabla V
concepts.definition: The (1 1) tensor field that maps a basis vector e_beta to the vector d V/dx^beta; its components in any coordinates are V^alpha_;beta, which equal plain partial derivatives in Cartesian coordinates and can be computed either with that system's Christoffel symbols or by tensor transformation from Cartesian components.
concepts.how_introduced: Obtained by treating the free derivative index beta as an input slot. Stressed as the foundation of all later work: one geometric object, many component representations.
concepts.notes: Exercise 5.10 asks for a proof that it is a (1 1) tensor.

concepts.name: covariant derivative of a scalar
concepts.definition: Because a scalar does not refer to any basis, its covariant derivative is just its gradient one-form, with components equal to partial derivatives.
concepts.how_introduced: Short argument: covariant and partial derivatives differ only through basis changes, which a scalar lacks.

concepts.name: divergence in curvilinear coordinates
concepts.definition: The scalar obtained by contracting nabla V on its two indices; since contraction is basis independent it equals the Cartesian divergence, and in polar coordinates it is (1/r) d(r V^r)/dr + d V^theta/d theta.
concepts.how_introduced: Link-up with familiar vector calculus before more theory: contract, use Gamma^alpha_r alpha = 1/r and Gamma^alpha_theta alpha = 0, and recognize the known formula (in coordinate-basis components).
concepts.notes: Differs in appearance from textbook formula 5.87 only because of basis choice.

concepts.name: Laplacian in polar coordinates
concepts.definition: nabla^2 phi = (1/r) d/dr (r d phi/dr) + (1/r^2) d^2 phi/d theta^2, the divergence of the vector gradient, identically equal to the Cartesian sum of second derivatives.
concepts.how_introduced: Advertised at the end of §5.1 as a bonus that demystifies a memorized formula; obtained by first raising the gradient one-form to a vector (since divergence needs a vector) and inserting into the polar divergence.
prerequisites: inverse metric and the vector gradient

concepts.name: covariant derivative of one-forms and higher-rank tensors
concepts.definition: For a one-form, the partial derivative of the components minus the one-form contracted with the Christoffel symbols (Eq. 5.63); for any tensor, add to the partial derivative one Christoffel term per index, with plus sign for upper indices (treated like vectors) and minus sign for lower indices (treated like one-forms), the derivative index always last on Gamma.
concepts.how_introduced: Uses the scalar p_alpha V^alpha: expand its gradient with the ordinary product rule, replace V^alpha_,beta by V^alpha_;beta minus the Gamma term, and argue that the leftover bracket multiplying an arbitrary vector must be a tensor component. Sign explained: basis one-forms change oppositely to basis vectors because their contraction is a constant Kronecker delta. Then general formulas for (0 2), (2 0), (1 1) tensors are displayed as a systematic pattern.

concepts.name: Leibniz rule for covariant derivative
concepts.definition: Covariant differentiation of products and contractions obeys the ordinary product rule, e.g. the derivative of a one-form contracted with a vector equals the derivative of the one-form contracted with the vector plus the one-form contracted with the derivative of the vector.
concepts.how_introduced: Falls out of the one-form derivation; justified because in Cartesian coordinates nabla reduces to partial differentiation of components, where the ordinary product rule holds.
prerequisites: covariant derivative of one-forms and higher-rank tensors

concepts.name: Cartesian-then-tensor-equation argument
aliases: prove it in a convenient frame, then generalize
tensor equation valid in one basis is valid in all
concepts.definition: If an equation relating components of tensors holds in one coordinate system (typically Cartesian, where Gamma = 0 and g = delta), then because both sides transform identically it holds in every coordinate system.
concepts.how_introduced: Used for the equality of divergences, symmetry of the second derivative of a scalar, and especially metric compatibility, where the verbal argument is repeated explicitly in primed and unprimed index equations for readers who need it.
concepts.notes: In curved spaces the role of Cartesian coordinates is taken by local inertial (locally flat) coordinates.

concepts.name: metric compatibility
concepts.definition: The covariant derivative of the metric tensor vanishes in every coordinate system; equivalently, lowering an index commutes with covariant differentiation.
concepts.how_introduced: Argued from Cartesian coordinates, where a vector and its one-form have equal components and nabla is partial differentiation, so nabla of the one-form equals g applied to nabla V; this tensor equation holds everywhere; comparing with the product rule on V_alpha = g_alpha mu V^mu for arbitrary V gives nabla g = 0. Then checked in polar coordinates on g_theta theta;r, which vanishes 'almost magically' but, the book insists, necessarily. A perspective paragraph promises the result persists in curved spaces.
prerequisites: covariant derivative of one-forms and higher-rank tensors

concepts.name: symmetry of Christoffel symbols
aliases: torsion-free connection in a coordinate basis
concepts.definition: In any coordinate basis the Christoffel symbols are symmetric in their two lower indices.
concepts.how_introduced: Proof via an arbitrary scalar: nabla nabla phi has components phi_,beta;alpha that are symmetric in Cartesian coordinates, hence in all; expanding with the one-form rule and using commuting partial derivatives leaves (Gamma^mu_alpha beta - Gamma^mu_beta alpha) phi_,mu = 0 for all phi.
prerequisites: covariant derivative of one-forms and higher-rank tensors
concepts.notes: Fails in noncoordinate bases (§5.5); see commutation coefficients in Exercise 5.20.

concepts.name: Christoffel symbols from the metric
concepts.definition: In a coordinate basis, each Christoffel symbol is one half of the inverse metric contracted with a combination of first partial derivatives of the metric: two index-permuted derivatives added and a third subtracted (Eq. 5.75).
concepts.how_introduced: Described as some advanced index gymnastics: write metric compatibility with three cyclic index permutations, add two and subtract the third, cancel antisymmetric combinations using symmetry of Gamma, divide by 2 and contract with the inverse metric. Checked on Gamma^theta_r theta = 1/r in polars; reader urged to memorize it because it carries over unchanged to curved spaces.
prerequisites: inverse metric and the vector gradient
concepts.notes: Valid only in coordinate bases.

concepts.name: non-tensorial nature of Christoffel symbols
concepts.definition: For fixed alpha, Gamma^mu_alpha beta are the components of the (1 1) tensor nabla e_alpha, but there is no single (1 2) tensor with components Gamma^mu_alpha beta, so they do not transform by the tensor law (they vanish in Cartesian coordinates yet not in polar); only the full combination V^beta_,alpha + V^mu Gamma^beta_mu alpha is tensorial.
concepts.how_introduced: Refines the common textbook slogan: a coordinate change replaces the basis vectors, so the relevant tensors nabla e_beta' are different tensors, not new components of the old ones.
concepts.notes: Exercise 5.17 works out the inhomogeneous transformation explicitly.

concepts.name: orthonormal basis
concepts.definition: A basis whose vectors satisfy e_alpha-hat . e_beta-hat = delta; for polar coordinates e_r-hat = e_r, e_theta-hat = e_theta/r, with dual one-forms omega^r-hat = d-tilde-r and omega^theta-hat = r d-tilde-theta. Carets on indices denote orthonormal components.
concepts.how_introduced: Built by normalizing the polar coordinate basis, motivated by convenience and by its universal use in vector-calculus texts.

concepts.name: noncoordinate basis
concepts.definition: A field of basis vectors that is not the coordinate basis of any coordinate system; in such a basis phi_,mu = d-tilde-phi(e_mu) is not a partial derivative with respect to a coordinate, Christoffel symbols need not be symmetric, and the metric formula for Gamma fails.
concepts.how_introduced: Existence question posed for the orthonormal polar basis and answered through the one-forms: if they were gradients of some eta, mixed partials of eta would have to agree, and they do not. Then general remarks on which results survive, with the promise that the book rarely uses such bases.
concepts.notes: Orthonormal frames (tetrads) become important in later chapters for observers, but the book mostly avoids them.

concepts.name: integrability conditions
concepts.definition: A set of one-forms omega^alpha-bar = Lambda^alpha-bar_beta d-tilde-x^beta is a coordinate basis only if each Lambda^alpha-bar_beta is a partial derivative of some function, which requires d Lambda^alpha-bar_beta / dx^gamma = d Lambda^alpha-bar_gamma / dx^beta.
concepts.how_introduced: Generalizes the mixed-partials failure found for the orthonormal polar basis; notes that an arbitrary position-dependent transformation matrix typically violates it.
prerequisites: transformation matrices for vectors and one-forms

concepts.name: physical versus coordinate components
concepts.definition: A vector with polar coordinate-basis components (a, b) has orthonormal-basis components (a, r b); formulas like the divergence look different in the two bases while describing the same scalar.
concepts.how_introduced: Used to reconcile Eq. 5.56 with the divergence formula in vector-calculus books (Eq. 5.87), removing an apparent contradiction.
concepts.notes: The term 'physical components' is not used by Schutz; it is the common engineering name.

concepts.name: Riemann curvature tensor
concepts.definition: The tensor that quantifies how much parallelism fails in a curved space, i.e. the departure from Euclid's parallel axiom.
concepts.how_introduced: Only named in the look-ahead as the missing measure to be developed next chapter.
prerequisites: flat versus curved geometry via parallelism

concepts.name: Rindler coordinates
aliases: coordinates of a uniformly accelerated observer
concepts.definition: Coordinates (lambda, a) on one quadrant of the Minkowski t-x plane defined by t = a sinh lambda, x = a cosh lambda, adapted to uniformly accelerated observers; orthogonal, singular on the light lines |x| = |t|.
concepts.how_introduced: Only in Exercise 5.21, as an application of curvilinear-coordinate machinery to SR, with a remark that the boundary lines resemble black-hole horizons.

key_equations.name: Gravitational redshift from energy conservation
key_equations.meaning: A photon rising a height h loses the fraction gh of its energy and frequency, as required to prevent a perpetual-motion cycle.
key_equations.symbols: E, E': photon energy at bottom and top; nu, nu': frequencies; m: rest mass dropped; g: gravitational acceleration; h: tower height (units c = 1).

key_equations.name: No redshift in a freely falling frame
key_equations.meaning: The Doppler blueshift seen by a frame that has fallen for the light-travel time h exactly compensates the gravitational redshift to first order, so the falling observer measures the emitted frequency.
key_equations.symbols: gh: speed acquired by the falling frame during travel time h; nu: frequency in the freely falling frame; nu': frequency at top of apparatus.

key_equations.name: Polar coordinates and their increments
key_equations.latex: x = r\cos\theta,\ y = r\sin\theta;\qquad \Delta r = \cos\theta\,\Delta x + \sin\theta\,\Delta y,\quad \Delta\theta = -\frac{\sin\theta}{r}\Delta x + \frac{\cos\theta}{r}\Delta y
key_equations.meaning: Definition of polar coordinates and the first-order linear relation between polar and Cartesian displacements.
key_equations.symbols: r, theta: polar coordinates; x, y: Cartesian coordinates.

key_equations.name: Nonvanishing Jacobian
key_equations.meaning: Condition for (xi, eta) to label points uniquely near a point; where it fails the transformation is singular.
key_equations.symbols: xi, eta: new coordinates as functions of x, y.

key_equations.name: Vector transformation law in general coordinates
key_equations.meaning: Vector components transform like coordinate displacements, with a position-dependent matrix of partial derivatives.
key_equations.symbols: Primed indices: new coordinates (xi, eta); unprimed: Cartesian; indices take values 1, 2.

key_equations.name: Gradient one-form
key_equations.meaning: Defines a one-form from any scalar field by its partial derivatives in whatever coordinates are used.
key_equations.symbols: phi: scalar field.

key_equations.name: One-form transformation law
key_equations.meaning: One-form components transform with the inverse matrix (derivatives of old coordinates by new), summed on the first index as for a row vector; follows from the chain rule.
key_equations.symbols: Lambda^alpha_beta': one-form transformation matrix.

key_equations.name: Transformation matrices are inverses
key_equations.meaning: By the chain rule the vector and one-form transformation matrices multiply to the identity.

key_equations.name: Tangent vector as derivative operator
key_equations.meaning: The rate of change of a scalar along a parametrized curve splits into a one-form depending only on the field and a vector depending only on the curve.
key_equations.symbols: s: curve parameter; V: tangent vector.

key_equations.name: Polar basis vectors
key_equations.meaning: Coordinate basis vectors of polar coordinates expressed in the constant Cartesian basis; e_theta scales with r.
key_equations.symbols: e_x, e_y: Cartesian basis vectors.

key_equations.name: Polar basis one-forms
key_equations.meaning: Basis one-forms of polar coordinates in the Cartesian one-form basis; they mirror ordinary calculus increments.

key_equations.label: (5.28a)-(5.28b)
key_equations.name: Magnitudes of polar bases
key_equations.meaning: The polar coordinate basis is not a unit basis; the theta basis vector grows with radius and the theta one-form shrinks.

key_equations.name: Polar metric components
key_equations.meaning: Metric components in any basis are dot products of basis vectors; for polar coordinates they are diag(1, r^2).
key_equations.symbols: g: Euclidean metric tensor, delta_alpha beta in Cartesian coordinates (Eq. 5.29).

key_equations.name: Polar line element
key_equations.meaning: Squared length of an infinitesimal displacement in polar coordinates, a compact display of metric components.
key_equations.symbols: dr, d theta: infinitesimal coordinate increments (not basis one-forms).

key_equations.name: Metric as a sum of basis tensor products
key_equations.meaning: The metric as a (0 2) tensor operator; fed the displacement vector in both slots it returns the line element.

key_equations.name: Inverse metric and vector gradient in polars
key_equations.meaning: Raising the index of the gradient changes its theta component by 1/r^2: vector and one-form components differ outside Cartesian coordinates.
key_equations.symbols: vec d phi: vector gradient; phi_,beta: one-form gradient components.

key_equations.label: (5.37a)-(5.37b)
key_equations.name: Derivatives of e_r
key_equations.meaning: The radial basis vector does not change along r but rotates with theta, its change pointing along e_theta.

key_equations.label: (5.38a)-(5.38b)
key_equations.name: Derivatives of e_theta
key_equations.meaning: e_theta grows linearly with r and turns inward as theta increases.

key_equations.name: Consistency check on constant e_x
key_equations.meaning: Derivatives of polar components are cancelled by derivatives of the polar basis, reproducing the constancy of e_x.

key_equations.name: Derivative of a vector field in a varying basis
key_equations.meaning: Product rule: the derivative of a vector includes both component changes and basis changes.

key_equations.name: Definition of Christoffel symbols
key_equations.meaning: Christoffel symbols are the basis components of the derivative of each basis vector along each coordinate.
key_equations.symbols: alpha: basis vector differentiated; beta: coordinate of differentiation; mu: component.

key_equations.name: Christoffel symbols of plane polar coordinates
key_equations.meaning: Complete table of connection coefficients for polar coordinates, allowing all derivative computations without Cartesian vectors.

key_equations.name: Factoring out the basis
key_equations.meaning: Substituting the Christoffel definition and relabelling dummy indices gives the components of the vector derivative.

key_equations.name: Covariant derivative of a vector
key_equations.meaning: Semicolon notation for the full components of the derivative of a vector field.
key_equations.symbols: comma: partial derivative; semicolon: covariant derivative.

key_equations.name: nabla V as a (1 1) tensor
key_equations.meaning: The covariant derivative components are the components of one tensor field, so they transform tensorially.

key_equations.name: Covariant derivative of a scalar
key_equations.meaning: For scalars the covariant derivative is the ordinary gradient.

key_equations.name: Invariance of the divergence
key_equations.meaning: Contraction of nabla V gives the same scalar in Cartesian and in arbitrary coordinates.
key_equations.symbols: Unprimed: Cartesian; primed: arbitrary coordinates.

key_equations.name: Contracted Christoffel symbols in polars
key_equations.meaning: Only the r contraction survives, producing the 1/r term in the divergence.

key_equations.name: Divergence in polar coordinates (coordinate basis)
key_equations.latex: V^\alpha{}_{;\alpha} = \frac{\partial V^r}{\partial r} + \frac{\partial V^\theta}{\partial\theta} + \frac{1}{r}V^r = \frac{1}{r}\frac{\partial}{\partial r}(rV^r) + \frac{\partial V^\theta}{\partial\theta}
key_equations.meaning: Divergence expressed with coordinate-basis polar components.

key_equations.name: Laplacian in polar coordinates
key_equations.meaning: Divergence of the vector gradient; derived rather than memorized, and identical to the Cartesian Laplacian.

key_equations.name: Product-rule route to the one-form derivative
key_equations.latex: \phi = p_\alpha V^\alpha,\quad \phi_{,\beta} = p_{\alpha,\beta}V^\alpha + p_\alpha V^\alpha{}_{,\beta} = \left(p_{\alpha,\beta} - p_\mu\Gamma^\mu{}_{\alpha\beta}\right)V^\alpha + p_\alpha V^\alpha{}_{;\beta}
key_equations.meaning: Since every other term is tensorial for arbitrary V, the bracket must be a tensor component.
key_equations.symbols: p: one-form; V: arbitrary vector.

key_equations.name: Covariant derivative of a one-form
key_equations.meaning: One-form components acquire a minus-sign Christoffel correction, reflecting that basis one-forms change oppositely to basis vectors.
